hook.text: Uber drivers also drive for Lyft. Sellers list on Amazon and eBay. Users often use both rivals.

buildup.text: Multi-homing is when users participate on multiple competing platforms simultaneously.

discovery.text: When multi-homing is easy, platforms can't build loyalty or charge high fees. Competition stays fierce.

twist.text: Platforms fight multi-homing with exclusivity deals. Spotify pays for podcast exclusives to keep you there.

climax.text: The ease of multi-homing determines whether a market becomes a monopoly or stays competitive.

punchline.text: If users can easily use both, neither platform wins outright.

details.summary: Multi-homing occurs when users actively participate on multiple competing platforms simultaneously. Drivers working for both Uber and Lyft, restaurants listed on DoorDash and Grubhub, and consumers shopping on Amazon and Walmart.com all multi-home across rival platforms.
details.whyItMatters: Multi-homing weakens platform lock-in and reduces winner-take-all dynamics. When switching between platforms is easy and costless, platforms must compete continuously on value rather than relying on captive user bases.
takeaways: Users on multiple competing platforms simultaneously weaken lock-in
Low switching costs and compatible standards enable multi-homing
Platforms invest in exclusive content and features to discourage multi-homing

faq.question: How do platforms try to prevent multi-homing by their users?
faq.answer: Exclusive content deals, loyalty programs, data that doesn't transfer, proprietary ecosystems, long-term contracts, and features only available to dedicated users. Apple's ecosystem integration makes multi-homing between iOS and Android costly and inconvenient.

faq.question: Is multi-homing good or bad for platforms?
faq.answer: Bad for dominant platforms because it prevents monopoly rents. Good for smaller platforms because it lowers barriers to user acquisition. Good for users and regulators because it maintains competitive pressure. The impact depends on which side you evaluate.
